analysis.one_liner: Imposes duties of care, loyalty, and confidentiality on online companies that collect personal data.
analysis.headline: The Data Care Act of 2025 was introduced in the Senate on December 18, 2025, backed by 12 Democrats and 2 Independents, and was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has received no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any online service that collects data identifying its users to act like a fiduciary toward that data. Companies would have to reasonably secure the data, tell users promptly when sensitive data is breached, refrain from using data in ways that foreseeably harm users, and only share or sell data to companies that sign on to the same duties. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general would enforce the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who uses the internet. Today, online companies can collect, share, and monetize personal data with almost no federal privacy rules beyond sector-specific laws like HIPAA. This bill would put users' personal information — health data, precise location, financial details, private messages — under enforceable duties that the company cannot waive in its terms of service, and it would let every state attorney general sue on residents' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Internet users whose data is collected and sold

how_it_helps.text: Requires online providers to reasonably secure personal data and promptly notify users of breaches involving sensitive data such as Social Security numbers, financial accounts, health information, biometrics, and precise location [S2].

Bars companies from using personal data in ways that benefit the company to the user's detriment and cause foreseeable physical or financial harm, or that would be highly offensive to a reasonable user [S2].
Prohibits selling or sharing personal data except with companies that contractually assume the same duties, and requires regular audits of those companies' data practices [S2].

Lets state attorneys general sue violators on behalf of residents, with penalties scaled to the number of days of noncompliance or the number of harmed users, and makes the rights unwaivable by contract [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Online companies that profit from collecting and monetizing user data — large platforms, advertising technology firms, and data brokers above all — would bear compliance costs and lose revenue from unrestricted data sharing. Some costs could eventually reach users as advertising-supported services adjust their business models.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data-driven online platforms and advertising companies

drawbacks.text: The 'online service provider' definition is very broad — any business that collects data linkable to a user over the internet — so small websites and apps could face real compliance costs, though the FTC may exempt categories of providers based on size, complexity, and the sensitivity of data handled [S2].

The duty of loyalty standard — barring uses that benefit the company to a user's 'detriment' — is broad and would be defined through FTC rulemaking and enforcement, creating uncertainty for businesses about which common practices (personalized ads, A/B testing, targeted promotions) are allowed [S2].

There is no private right of action: individual users could not sue on their own; enforcement runs only through the FTC and state attorneys general, so remedies depend on government prosecutors' priorities [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: consumers gain enforceable protections over data that today is largely governed by whatever a company's terms of service say, while data-driven companies bear compliance costs and lose some flexibility to monetize user information. The bill is deliberately built to allow flexibility — the FTC can tailor rules, exempt small providers, and expand breach-notification duties — and it leaves existing privacy laws untouched. Its main weakness is that without a private right of action, protection depends on FTC and state attorney general enforcement. On balance, it is a meaningful consumer protection with a real but manageable compliance cost, and its principal burden falls on companies whose revenue depends on extensive data collection.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on December 18, 2025; the committee has not held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor, and nothing has happened since.

narrative.text: Sen. Brian Schatz introduced the Data Care Act of 2025 on December 18, 2025, joined by 14 cosponsors — 12 Democrats and 2 Independents [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, which is its only action to date [S4].
No Republican senators have cosponsored the bill, and the Senate remains in session, so the bill could still move if the committee acts on it [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet. Online companies continue to collect and monetize user data under existing law, because the bill has not advanced beyond referral to committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nothing has happened yet; platforms keep current rules

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 14 cosponsors, all from his own caucus

for.name: Sen. Tammy Baldwin, Sen. Cory Booker, Sen. Tammy Duckworth, Sen. Dick Durbin, Sen. Angus King, Sen. Ed Markey group, Sen. Chris Murphy, Sen. Jeff Merkley, Sen. Bernie Sanders, Sen. Tina Smith, Sen. Peter Welch, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and others
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats or Independents; no Republican has signed on, so the bill's path likely runs through partisan negotiation that has not yet begun.

industries.industry: Online platforms and advertising technology (data-driven internet companies)
industries.note: The bill directly targets the business of collecting and monetizing user data: it bars selling or sharing personal data except under contracts that carry the same duties, and restricts uses that benefit the company to users' detriment. Data-driven ad targeting and data brokerage revenue are the main things constrained, and the constraint is the point — that is where consumer privacy gains come from.

industries.industry: Data brokers and secondary data markets
industries.note: These firms exist to trade individual identifying data; the duty of confidentiality and mandatory downstream contracts sharply limit what they can lawfully buy, sell, and share. Consumers gain because their data moves under enforceable duties rather than freely between intermediaries.

industries.industry: Small websites, apps, and online merchants
industries.note: The bill covers any online business that collects linkable user data, so small operators face compliance costs, though they could also benefit from stronger security expectations across the services they use. The FTC may exempt categories of providers based on size and the sensitivity of data they handle, which would ease the burden.

analysis.trajectory: A bill at this stage — introduced days before the end of the first session, with no hearing or markup scheduled and no Republican cosponsors — historically has a very low chance of becoming law. Its realistic path would require the Senate Commerce Committee to take it up in the second session and bipartisan negotiation to begin; until that happens, it is likely to sit in committee like most referred bills.
